1) Can you provide a single-page network boundary diagram that highlights tenant enclave boundaries, sidecar/ingress components, and external egress sinks (including any third-party service endpoints)?
2) We need an evidence packet that shows how you enforce non-broadcast egress (deny by default, allow-lists), and how you prevent cross-tenant KV or model cache leakage.
3) Please include a short threat summary (2–3 bullets) that maps realistic attack paths and your primary mitigations.

Markus — thanks for the clear ask. We're happy to provide both the diagram and a compact evidence packet. High level: Redwood's tenant isolation is enforced at three layers (network, process, and storage) and we run an allow-list egress model with regional egress sinks.

I've attached: network-boundary-20260719.png (single-page diagram) and egress-evidence-20260719.pdf (controls checklist + sample audit extracts). Key notes up front:
- Per-tenant enclosures: each customer gets an isolated runtime namespace with dedicated network policies and a per-tenant KV namespace; sidecars mediate all inbound/outbound model artifact pulls.
- Egress sinks: we use regional egress proxies with TLS termination and allow-listing; all egress requires signed service tokens and is logged to immutable audit streams.
- KV & cache: KV namespaces are keyed by tenant id; we use strict token scoping and runtime attestation to prevent cross-tenant access.

Proposed next steps: 30-minute walkthrough Wednesday 2026-07-21 10:00am PST. If that works I'll send a calendar invite.

- network-boundary-20260719.png (diagram stub)
- egress-evidence-20260719.pdf (controls checklist + sample logs)

Markus / team,

Quick clarifications to the packet Jonas just sent:
- The PNG is an export of our standard boundary view; the canonical editable version and layered overlays are in the Drive folder: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1aL_example_boundary_evidence
- The PDF includes redacted audit extracts showing allow-list lookups and egress proxy timestamps. For compliance review, we can also provide SIEM events for a 30‑day window under NDA.
- On KV isolation: in addition to tenant-scoped keys, we enforce read-only seals for model cache dirs by default; write operations require a signed runtime certificate issued per job.

Action items for us:
- I'll prepare a 1‑page mapping of the three highest-priority attack vectors (exposed below) and the controls owners.
- Jonas will host the walkthrough and show the runtime attestation flow.

Top attack vectors (short):
1) Stolen service tokens used to pivot to an egress proxy — mitigated by short token TTL + token binding to runtime instance id.
2) Model cache poisoning via artifact repo — mitigated by signed manifests + content-addressable storage + provenance checks.
3) Cross-tenant inference leaks via shared sidecar pathing — mitigated by per-tenant namespaces + enforced process isolation and network policies.

I'll attach a DocuSign link for the standard NDA if you'd like SIEM extracts.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Director, Security Solutions — Redwood Inference

1) Network policy proof: we'll show iptables/ebpf policy snapshots for a sample tenant (tenant-id: alpha-test-01) and an allow-list table showing only internal controlplane and approved S3 endpoints.
2) Egress verification: we will perform an on-call live test (from the walkthrough environment) that attempts outbound to a non-allowlisted domain and show the proxy deny + logged event.
3) KV isolation: we'll share a short script that demonstrates a write attempt from a different tenant context that fails with an access-denied audit entry.

Attached in the packet are representative CLI commands and the audit snippet format. During the live session we'll run the deny test and capture the SIEM event hash.
